pillar_reactions.evidence: He volunteered his own proof of concept, unprompted, immediately after the mobility pillar was described: 'I stumbled upon Trevor's page, and I saw some of his stretches, and I started doing it, and just within a couple of weeks, the lower back pain just started to really go away, so I'm like, ah, it takes effort.' The strongest lived endorsement of the method anywhere in this batch — and it came from free content.

Tied it straight to his own values without being asked: 'we're fine-tuned machines, we're not designed to eat McDonald's every day... nutrition is something that's really important, it's something that I'm trying to be more conscientious about', and criticised the delivery-app food culture around him. He had earlier asked whether tracking calories was necessary and accepted the quality-over-quantity answer readily.

He had named accountability as his need before the pillar arrived — 'someone like a coach that could say, hey man, what's going on'— and then interrogated the mechanics rather than the value: whether there is an app or whether he should write it on paper, whether meal times are logged, and what exactly gets tracked. Engaged and practical. Notable that this is the pillar he most needs and the one the product he ultimately chose does not include.

anchors.raw: I did talk to Kim, and I did ask about the price, but, you know, didn't really get any answer on that... to be honest, I was thinking that this program was going to be something kind of like a school thing, you know, where it's going to be more of a group.
anchors.note: The decisive anchor, and it was set before the call by the absence of an answer. He asked the setter what it cost, was not told, and filled the gap himself with a group-community price of roughly $200 a month. $6,000 then landed against an anchor thirty times smaller. He described the reaction plainly afterwards: 'The first one I was like, damn, like, it blew me out of the water.'

anchors.raw: recently, you know, I stumbled upon Trevor's page, and I saw some of his stretches, and I started doing it, and just within a couple of weeks, the lower back pain just started to really go away
anchors.note: His one concrete, recent, verifiable win from this provider came free. He also owns the kettlebells and keeps a gym membership on an annual plan specifically because it is cheaper. Everything in his experience says the marginal value of paying is small.

anchors.raw: I do take dancing lessons on my free time, and could I learn how to dance by myself and watch YouTube videos and everything? Yeah, I can, but if I go to an actual facility, you know, you have instructors, you have people that you dance with, you get better at it a lot quicker. So I'm thinking this is the exact same method.
anchors.note: He built the case for paid coaching himself, unprompted, and reinforced it with 'I don't want to go the cheapy method and like, I could figure it out.' The rep's response was to praise him — 'You're smart for saying that' — and then move on. This was the value bridge the price needed and it was left on the table twelve minutes before the price was named.

unmet_demand.want: A group or community programme at roughly $200 a month, which is what he came to the call expecting to buy
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The product exists and he was routed to the wrong call for it. He was booked onto a $6,000 one-to-one closer call, sat through thirty-three minutes of discovery and a full philosophy presentation, and only saw the product he actually wanted after refusing the one he was pitched. His reaction on seeing it — 'That seems more up my alley... Oh, 100%, like, without a doubt' — confirms the demand was real and servable throughout.

unmet_demand.want: Accountability — named twice as his primary need, ahead of structure and ahead of programming
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The tier he chose is explicitly the one without it. The rep drew the distinction himself: 'You just don't have the 24-7 support', and 'instead of paying for Trevor to do one-on-one with you, you're paying for Trevor's brain in a community.' A prospect whose stated failure mode is tapering off after two consistent months is buying the product that solves structure and not the one that solves adherence, and nobody named that trade-off out loud.
